title: Error Budget Allocation and Sprint Integration Playbook
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines how Redwood Inference teams allocate and consume error budget across product sprints, map error-budget consumption to capacity planning actions, and automate routine mitigation steps. It operationalizes error budgets so reliability is a first-class sprint input rather than an ad-hoc emergency item.

Audience: SREs, platform engineers, product managers, and engineering managers responsible for service SLOs, capacity, and release planning.

Background and principles

- Error budget (EB) = 1 - SLO target (measured over the configured window). Use a 30-day rolling window by default unless a service-specific policy states otherwise.
- Treat error budget as a finite, shared resource between feature velocity and reliability work.
- Prioritize automated mitigation and capacity changes before manual circuit breakers where possible.
- All actions must be observable and reversible; prefer canary + gradual rollbacks for risky changes.

Definitions and metrics

- SLI (example): successful-1s-latency — percentage of requests that return HTTP 200 within 1 second.
- SLO (example): 99.9% successful-1s-latency over 30 days.
- Error budget (example): 0.1% allowed error => EB_units = 0.1% * total_requests. We report EB as percentage and as remaining time-equivalent (e.g., X minutes of allowed downtime).
- Burn rate = (observed_error / EB_allocated) per time unit. Measured hourly and daily.

Service ownership and roles

- Service Owner (SO): product engineering manager for the specific service. Responsible for sprint-level prioritization of EB expenditure.
- Reliability Lead (RL): rotating SRE assigned to the service for the sprint. Responsible for monitoring, runbook execution, and coordinating mitigations.
- Capacity Owner (CO): platform/team owning autoscaling and resource provisioning for the service (often infra or platform team).
- On-call: primary/secondary SREs receiving alerts.

Label responsibilities in Jira tickets:

- reliability:bug — customer-facing errors tied to SLO breaches.
- reliability:investigation — load tests / perf investigations.
- reliability:work — planned architecture or infra work that consumes EB.

Error budget allocation model

1) Baseline allocation: each service gets a weekly EB pool derived from its 30-day EB converted into weekly units. This normalizes planning for sprint cadences. Example: SLO 99.9% over 30d -> EB = 0.1%. If average weekly requests = 10M, weekly EB units = 0.001 * 10M = 10k error requests. We then translate to time-equivalent using observed request rate during budgets.

2) Sprint reservation: teams may reserve up to 20% of a weekly EB pool for planned reliability experiments (e.g., chaos tests, migration cutovers). Anything beyond 20% requires explicit cross-team approval (SO + RL + CO).

3) Named allocations: for large events (launches, migrations), request a named EB allocation document (template below) 2 weeks in advance. This becomes an auditable override with mitigation and rollback plan.

Automation and tool integrations

- Dashboard: Every service must have an EB dashboard in Grafana showing current burn rate, remaining EB%, and 1h/6h/24h burn windows. Panels must include: requests/s, error count, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), and active mitigations.
- Alerts: Two-tier alerting model: 
  - advisory (no page): EB_burn_rate_1h > 3x for 1h -> slack #sre-advisory and service channel notification.
  - paged (page): EB_burn_rate_1h > 8x OR remaining_EB < 5% -> page primary on-call.
- Automation hooks: Alert actions should trigger the following in order (scripted via ops-tooling):
  1) run automated Canary traffic shift to fallback model/region (if configured) (CLI example below).
  2) enable temporary rate-limit policy for non-critical routes (defined in routing config).
  3) open a Jira incident ticket with EB tags and pre-filled template.

CLI snippet: shift traffic to fallback region

- Example command (ops-tool):
  ops-tool route shift --service ${SERVICE} --from-region us-east-1 --to-region us-west-2 --percent 50 --reason "EB burn 1h > 3x"

- Example command: enable route rate-limit
  ops-tool routing apply --service ${SERVICE} --route "/api/v1/model/embeddings" --limit 1000/min --window 60s --reason "EB mitigation"

Runbook: immediate actions for on-call when EB alert pages

1) Acknowledge page and post status in service channel with EB summary (remaining %, 1h burn, root-suspect if known).
2) RL runs quick triage: check top-5 endpoints by error and latency in Grafana + recent deploys in Deployments dashboard.
2a) If a recent deploy (<30m) is implicated, trigger deploy rollback or pause rollout (prefer pause for canary).
3) If spike is capacity-related (CPU/GPU saturation, 95th queue depth > threshold), contact CO to enact autoscale policy or capacity addition. Use capacity playbook steps below.
4) If traffic skew or 3rd-party degradation, enable route-level rate limits and apply client-side backoff recommendations.
5) If mitigation is to shift traffic, use ops-tool commands above to move incremental percents every 5 minutes while monitoring latency and error.
6) Update Jira incident with hypothesis, mitigations, and next steps. Every 30 minutes add a timestamped note.

Capacity playbook (mapping EB burn into capacity actions)

Thresholds (default, service-specific overrides allowed in service config):
- CPU/GPU saturation definition: sustained > 80% for 10 minutes across >= 50% of hosts.
- Queue depth trigger: p95 request queue time > 200ms or queue length > 100 for 5m.
- Autoscale policy: target CPU 60-70%; max burst up to 200% reserved capacity for 15 minutes.

Actions by situation:
- Short burst (burn rate 3x-8x, < 1 hour): apply emergency autoscale (if available), enable batching heuristics via feature flag, and apply rate limits on non-critical routes.
- Sustained high burn (>8x for >1 hour or remaining_EB < 5%): enact capacity surge play — CO to provision additional pods/instances and/or request Dedicated GPU burst (submit sync ticket to capacity queue).
- No autoscale available / capacity caps reached: initiate traffic shaping + degrade non-essential model features (e.g., lower precision or smaller model variant) automatically using model-routing rules.

Example capacity surge request template (Jira):
- Summary: Capacity surge request — ${SERVICE} — ${reason}
- Requested by: CO or RL
- Impact window: start/end
- Resources requested: x extra instances (type), GPUs, disk IO
- Rollback plan: deprovision steps and monitoring thresholds
- Approval: SO + infra lead

Sprint-level integration and prioritization

- Sprints are primary planning unit (2 or 3 weeks). At sprint planning:
  1) RL presents current EB status and projection for sprint (graph: projected remaining EB by sprint end).
  2) SO and EM decide on how much EB to budget for planned feature work. Recommended: reserve 30%-50% of weekly EB for unplanned incidents; allocate the remainder to feature and planned infra work.
  3) All tickets that may consume EB must include an estimated EB impact line in the ticket (low/medium/high) with a short justification.
  4) Tickets that are >20% of weekly EB require explicit RL + SO sign-off and a rollback/runbook attached.

- Sprint retrospective: include "reliability outcomes" section where EB overspend, mitigations, and root cause items are captured as action items with owners and due dates.

Reliability initiatives and continuous improvement

- Quarterly reliability plan: each service should produce a 90-day reliability initiative linked to EB goals (e.g., reduce p99 latency by 20%, add prefix cache to reduce token costs).
- Initiative cadence: plan -> implementation -> eval -> measurement. Each initiative should declare expected EB savings (estimated reduction in EB consumption).

Incident review and postmortem standards related to EB

- Any incident that consumes >10% of a weekly EB or triggers a page must have a postmortem within 5 business days. Postmortem template must include: timeline, detection, mitigation, root cause, EB impact (absolute and relative), lessons learned, and action items with owners and due dates.
- Postmortems are reviewed in the Reliability Review board monthly. Action item owners must update status weekly.

Operational tooling and recommended configs

- Grafana dashboards: include panels for EB remaining (rolling 30d & weekly), 1h/6h/24h burn rates, service top endpoints, and current mitigations.
- Prometheus rules (example):
  - alert: EBHighBurnRate1h
    expr: (increase(slo_errors_total[1h]) / (slo_error_budget_total / 30)) > 3
    for: 10m
    labels: {severity: "advisor"}
  - alert: EBCritical
    expr: (increase(slo_errors_total[1h]) / (slo_error_budget_total / 30)) > 8 OR (slo_remaining_percent < 5)
    for: 5m
    labels: {severity: "page"}

- Ops-tooling: every service must implement ops-tool hooks for: traffic shift, rate-limit application, model-variant switch, and opening Jira incidents. Document required flags in the service runtime config.

Templates and artifacts

- Named allocation doc template (short):
  - Service:
  - Reason:
  - Time window:
  - Expected EB usage (% of weekly pool):
  - Rollout steps and canary plan:
  - Mitigations and rollback criteria:
  - Approvals:

- Quick incident ticket template (auto-populated):
  - Summary: EB alert — ${SERVICE} — ${region}
  - Severity: P1/P2
  - Observed EB change: current %, burn rate 1h/24h
  - Immediate mitigations: (list)

Examples and scenarios

1) Canary deploy causing 2x burn for 20 minutes: pause rollout and revert; mark deploy ticket with "reliability:investigation". No capacity change.
2) Sudden traffic spike from a partner causes sustained 6x burn for 2 hours: enable autoscale, apply route rate-limits, and open surge capacity request. Post-incident, negotiate partner-side throttling and add a dedicated integration test in CI.
3) Model degradation due to 3rd-party embedding infra: switch to degraded model variant (lower precision) using model-routing rule; this reduces EB consumption by reducing inference latency and error.

Governance and exceptions

- Emergency overrides: CEO/CTO can grant cross-service EB credits for major launches; all overrides must be recorded and timeboxed.
- Long-term exceptions (exceeding 4x weekly EB for multiple weeks) require board-level reliability plan and allocation from product portfolio.

Appendices

A. Calculating time-equivalent EB: convert allowed error requests into minutes of downtime by dividing allowed error requests by average requests/minute.

B. Runbook quick reference (short):
  - EB advisory: notify RL -> run quick triage -> monitor for 1h
  - EB page: acknowledge -> shift traffic to fallback -> enable rate-limits -> request capacity surge if needed -> document in Jira
\C. Helpful links:
  - Deployments dashboard: https://grafana.internal.redwood/deploys
  - EB dashboards: https://grafana.internal.redwood/eb_dashboards
